notes: Every trait is scored AS OF the draft: the projection published for that season, and only actuals from before it.
The within-draft correlation removes the (season, round) mean first, so shared late-round drift is not read as a personal trait.

Per-pick traits are weighted 0.8^(round-1) across the whole draft. Position is an unweighted share of the finished roster: an earlier version took it over rounds 1-5 and concluded positional preference does not persist, which is the wrong window for a question about what a manager ends up with.
Family-wise p is from 2000 permutations of which manager each season's numbers belong to, across all fourteen cells at once. Significance is that number, not the per-cell p.
The within-draft split is at round 5, over drafts of 16 rounds.
overturns: Positional preference was measured over rounds 1-5 and reported as not persisting. That is the wrong window: which position a manager takes early is dictated by the board, while how many tight ends he ends up with is a choice, and over the whole draft it is the most persistent thing here (+0.69). The pick model's six per-manager position dummies were the right instinct at the wrong resolution -- what carries is a target roster shape, and inside a draft a manager moves AGAINST it as he fills up, which is why a preference-shaped feature had the sign backwards.
question: A manager's habits should help predict his next pick -- but which habits, and does history predict them or does the draft in front of us?
title: Owner tendencies: which ones persist, and on which axis
